description: Religious teachings on violence, terrorism, Just War Theory and modern warfare.
content_html:
What Do Religions Say About Violence?

Most religious traditions do not treat violence as morally neutral. They recognise that life has value and that harming others requires serious justification. Yet they also acknowledge that the world is not always peaceful, and that believers must think carefully about when, if ever, force is permissible. This tension between the ideal of peace and the reality of conflict runs through all the major world religions.

Christianity teaches that human beings are made in the image of God, and that taking life is therefore a grave matter. Jesus said in Matthew 5:43–44: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” This command to love even enemies is central to the Christian ethic of nonviolence. However, many Christians have also concluded that some forms of force can be justified in extreme circumstances — the tradition of Just War Theory emerged precisely to answer that question.

Key Fact

The prophet Micah taught that one day nations would “beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Micah 4:3). This verse is widely used in religious peace traditions to describe the ideal of a world without war. It appears in the Hebrew scriptures and is cited across Jewish and Christian traditions alike.

Terrorism and Religion

Terrorism is the deliberate use of violence against civilians to cause fear and achieve political or ideological ends. The causes of terrorism are complex: they include political grievances, economic marginalisation, cultural humiliation, and extremist ideologies that claim divine sanction for violence. Religious extremism is one factor, but sociologists and security analysts stress that it is rarely the only cause.

The relationship between religion, politics and terrorism in the 21st century is deeply contested. Acts of terror have been committed in the name of Christianity, Islam, Judaism and other faiths, yet the overwhelming majority of believers in each tradition condemn terrorism absolutely. Religious leaders across traditions have consistently argued that targeting innocent civilians is never justified and that extremist groups misuse and distort their scriptures. For example, mainstream Islamic scholars argue that the killing of innocent non-combatants is strictly forbidden under Islamic law, and that terrorist groups who claim religious legitimacy have abandoned the authentic teaching of their tradition.

Just War Theory

Just War Theory is the most influential framework Christians have used to think about war. The medieval philosopher and theologian Thomas Aquinas drew together earlier ideas and identified three core conditions for a just war in his Summa Theologiae: first, the war must be declared by a legitimate authority (not a private individual); second, there must be a just cause (such as defence against aggression); and third, the warriors must have a right intention (seeking peace and avoiding personal gain or cruelty).

Thomas Aquinas outlined three conditions in the Summa Theologiae: (1) legitimate authority — only a ruler with responsibility for the common good can declare war; (2) just cause — the cause must be the defence of the innocent or righting a grave wrong; (3) right intention — the aim must be to achieve good or avoid evil, not to satisfy ambition or hatred. Later Catholic tradition expanded these into a fuller set of criteria found in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 2309), adding principles such as last resort, proportionality, and a reasonable chance of success. Protestant traditions have generally adopted similar criteria. An important but distinct concept is jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war) — the idea that even a just war must be fought in a just manner, sparing non-combatants and avoiding disproportionate destruction.

Holy War

Holy War is a concept found across traditions. In the Hebrew Bible, passages such as Joshua 8:1 describe God commanding the Israelites to fight and promising victory. In early Christian history, the Crusades were presented as holy wars to reclaim Jerusalem. The concept of holy war differs from Just War in that it claims divine authorisation rather than depending on moral criteria. Most modern religious thinkers are deeply uncomfortable with the idea of a war that claims God’s direct command, partly because it has historically been used to justify atrocities.

Key Fact

Just War Theory requires war to meet morally rational criteria such as just cause, legitimate authority and right intention. Holy War claims direct divine command and is not assessed by the same rational conditions. Many modern religious thinkers reject Holy War as too easily abused, while accepting that Just War criteria may sometimes permit defensive force.

Conventional warfare involves armies engaging one another directly on battlefields. Just War criteria were developed with this kind of conflict in mind. Technological warfare, including drone strikes and “surgical” precision attacks, raises new moral questions: is a strike on a single target that risks civilian casualties ever proportionate? Does removing the human cost from one side change the moral calculus? Religious ethicists disagree. Some argue that precision weapons can actually reduce civilian deaths and are therefore more just; others argue that the ease of using remote weapons lowers the moral threshold for violence.

Apocalyptic warfare, most seriously represented by nuclear weapons, challenges Just War Theory fundamentally. The indiscriminate destruction of nuclear bombs makes it impossible to distinguish combatants from civilians, and the scale of potential harm means no military objective could be proportionate. Many religious traditions, including many Catholic bishops and Quaker communities, have argued that nuclear weapons can never be used justly and have called for disarmament. The book of Joel 3:9–11 was used in early Christian debates about war: “Beat your ploughshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears” — ironically reversing Micah’s vision of peace into a call for battle, illustrating how scripture can be read in contrasting ways.

Religious Responses to War

Different religious communities and denominations respond to war in different ways. Most agree that peace is the ideal and that war should be a last resort. Many Christians point to Jesus’s teaching in Matthew 5:43–44 — “Love your enemies” — as a reason for caution about any resort to violence. Others emphasise the responsibility to protect the innocent and argue that allowing evil to go unchecked is itself a moral failure. Islamic teaching, similarly, affirms that life is sacred and that taking it unlawfully is among the most serious sins, yet it also recognises the legitimacy of defending the community against aggression. Both traditions therefore contain threads of both nonviolence and regulated force.
exam_tip_html: For “Outline” questions (3 marks), give three distinct points without padding. For “Explain” questions (6 marks), develop each point with reasoning and a supporting religious teaching. The 15-mark “Discuss” question on this topic often uses a stimulus such as “‘Religion only ever causes violence.’ Discuss.” — prepare both sides with named examples. The most common student error is confusing Just War Theory with Holy War: Just War uses moral criteria; Holy War claims divine command. Accurate spelling of technical terms like “pacifism,” “Just War,” and “apocalyptic warfare” is assessed on your extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religious traditions generally teach that violence is serious, life is sacred, and war should be a last resort — but most also allow that defensive force can sometimes be justified.
  • Just War Theory (developed especially by Thomas Aquinas) requires three core conditions: legitimate authority, just cause, and right intention. Modern technological and nuclear warfare raises new challenges that these criteria struggle to address.
  • Holy War differs from Just War by claiming direct divine sanction rather than ethical criteria, and is widely viewed by modern religious thinkers as open to abuse.

practice_questions.text: State one condition that Thomas Aquinas identified as necessary for a just war.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: legitimate authority / just cause / right intention. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the term 'Holy War'.
practice_questions.marks: Credit responses that identify: a war believed to be commanded or sanctioned by God (1 mark); fought in defence of religious belief or sacred territory, claiming divine authorisation rather than relying on human moral criteria (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline three religious teachings that could be used to argue against violence.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points, for example: Jesus's command to 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:43-44) suggests violence towards others is wrong; Micah 4:3 envisions nations beating swords into ploughshares, suggesting peace is the religious ideal; mainstream Islamic scholars teach that killing innocent civilians is strictly forbidden under Islamic law and is a grave sin. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Just War Theory is challenged by modern forms of warfare.
practice_questions.marks: Credit two developed points, for example: Technological warfare using drones raises the question of proportionality — precision weapons may reduce civilian casualties but the ease of deploying them may lower the moral threshold for using force, which Just War's 'last resort' condition resists (3 marks). Apocalyptic or nuclear warfare cannot satisfy Just War's requirement to spare non-combatants, because nuclear weapons cause indiscriminate mass destruction — no military objective could be proportionate to this harm, leading many religious leaders to call for nuclear disarmament (3 marks). [6 marks — 3 marks per point: 1 basic, 2 developed, 3 developed with religious reference]

practice_questions.text: 'Religion always causes violence rather than preventing it.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Religious language has been used to legitimise terrorism and atrocity throughout history, from the Crusades to modern extremist groups who claim divine sanction; the concept of Holy War can encourage believers to think ordinary moral limits do not apply when God commands violence; passages such as Joel 3:9-11 and Joshua 8:1 have been used to justify aggressive war; religious identity differences can harden divisions between communities, raising the risk of conflict.

Arguments against: Most religious traditions explicitly teach that violence is a last resort or is forbidden: Jesus commands love of enemies (Matthew 5:43-44); Micah 4:3 envisions a world without weapons; Islamic scholars condemn terrorism as a distortion of faith; Just War Theory was developed precisely to restrain rather than encourage war; religious peacemakers such as Gandhi, Desmond Tutu and Martin Luther King Jr used their faith as the motivation for non-violent resistance; many religious organisations run reconciliation and aid programmes in conflict zones.

Mastering: Both sides are fully developed with named sources, explicit weighing of the arguments and a justified conclusion (e.g. religion is sometimes misused to justify violence but its dominant teachings and most prominent practitioners have worked for peace).
Secure: Both sides covered with some named teachings and a conclusion.
Developing: Some attempt at both sides; limited use of religious evidence.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; little or no use of religious teaching. [15 marks + SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Outline three differences between conventional, technological and apocalyptic warfare.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three distinct points: Conventional warfare involves armies in direct combat and was the context in which Just War Theory was originally developed; technological warfare uses drones or precision weapons at a distance, raising questions about proportionality and the ease of deploying force; apocalyptic warfare, such as nuclear weapons, involves indiscriminate mass destruction that cannot distinguish between combatants and civilians. [3 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which Christian thinker is most associated with developing Just War Theory in the medieval period?
Which of the following is NOT one of the three conditions Thomas Aquinas identified for a just war?
Micah 4:3 teaches that nations should beat their swords into _____, expressing the religious ideal of peace.
Warfare using drones and precision-guided weapons to carry out targeted strikes from a distance is called _____ warfare.
Match each type of warfare to its key feature:
right: Armies engaging directly in combat on a battlefield
Drone strikes and precision weapons deployed at a distance
Nuclear weapons causing indiscriminate mass destruction

flashcard_questions.q: What are Thomas Aquinas's three conditions for a just war?
flashcard_questions.a: Legitimate authority, just cause, and right intention.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Holy War differ from Just War Theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Holy War claims direct divine command; Just War requires morally rational criteria.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Micah 4:3 say about swords?
flashcard_questions.a: Nations will beat their swords into ploughshares — an image of lasting peace.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Jesus teach about enemies in Matthew 5:43-44?
flashcard_questions.a: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.
Using violence or threats against civilians to achieve political or ideological goals.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do religious thinkers struggle to justify nuclear warfare using Just War Theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Nuclear weapons cannot spare non-combatants, so they cannot be proportionate.
War fought between organised armed forces engaging directly in combat.

flashcard_questions.q: What moral question does drone warfare raise for Just War Theory?
flashcard_questions.a: Whether precision strikes are proportionate and whether easy use lowers the moral threshold.
A framework setting moral conditions under which war can be ethically justified.
A medieval Dominican theologian who systematised Just War thinking in his Summa Theologiae.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Joel 3:9-11 describe, and how does it contrast with Micah 4:3?
flashcard_questions.a: Joel calls for ploughshares to be beaten into swords — the reverse of Micah's vision of peace.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do most religious traditions reject terrorism?
flashcard_questions.a: Deliberately targeting innocent civilians is condemned across all major religious traditions.

glossary_terms.definition: A moral framework, developed especially by Thomas Aquinas, setting conditions under which going to war and how it is fought may be ethically justified.
The use of violence or threat of violence, typically targeting civilians, to achieve political, ideological or religious goals.
Dominican friar and philosopher (1225-1274) who systematised Christian Just War thinking in his Summa Theologiae.
A war believed to be commanded or sanctioned by God, fought in defence of religious belief or sacred territory.
War fought between organised armed forces in direct combat, typically with soldiers, tanks and aircraft.
Warfare using advanced technology such as drones and precision-guided weapons to carry out targeted strikes from a distance.
Warfare involving weapons of mass destruction, particularly nuclear weapons, capable of catastrophic destruction on a global scale.
